summary:
We built a web tool, live at spherex.peykan.ai, that turns NASA SPHEREx infrared images into a sky "blink" anyone can use. Type a name or coordinates, and the tool fetches every SPHEREx image of that spot, groups the images by survey visit and animates them, so moving and changing objects stand out. Users can subtract or add images taken at different times, step through all 102 SPHEREx wavelengths, and click any star to see its spectrum and brightness over time. Gaia and WISE catalogue stars are overlaid at each image's date, and pixels the pipeline flags as contaminated are clearly marked.

Our innovation is automatic moving-source detection. It finds sources that move between visits and checks them against Gaia. A mover with no Gaia match is flagged as a discovery candidate: the tool recovers the brown dwarf WISE 0855 this way, at 7.5″ per year.

This matters because SPHEREx maps the whole sky every six months in infrared light. That is where cold, nearby brown dwarfs that Gaia misses are brightest. The tool picks up new data releases automatically and accepts users' own FITS images.
details:
What it does and how it works

SPHEREx Sky Motion Explorer is a free website (spherex.peykan.ai) for finding moving and changing objects in NASA SPHEREx data. A user enters an object name or sky coordinates. The tool then:

  1. Finds every SPHEREx image of that position in the NASA/IPAC archive (IRSA). It reads only the needed pixels and quality flags directly from the public archive copy on Amazon S3.
  2. Aligns the images onto a common north-up grid at SPHEREx's native 6.15″ pixels and removes the background glow.
  3. Groups exposures into survey visits ("epochs"), about six months apart, and stacks each visit, weighting every exposure by its noise.
  4. Animates the result. Users blink between visits, single exposures, or all 102 SPHEREx wavelengths (a spectrum played as a movie).

On top of the blink view:

  • Image arithmetic: subtract or add any chosen sets of visits, or compare each visit with the average, so motion and brightness changes stand out.
  • Catalogue overlays: Gaia DR3 (optical) and CatWISE2020 (infrared) stars, each moved to the date of the frame using its catalogued motion, with SIMBAD names on hover.
  • Contamination map: shows pixels the SPHEREx pipeline flags as ghosts, halos, streaks or crosstalk, with counts per flag.
  • Spectrum and light curve: click any star to see its spectrum per visit and its brightness over time, compared at matched wavelengths. Both can be downloaded as CSV.
  • Reference images: unWISE, Legacy Survey or the interactive Aladin Lite sky atlas, shown beside the blink view.
  • Sharing: a side-by-side PNG export, shareable links, and an embed mode for other websites.

Moving-source detection, our discovery engine. The tool automatically:

  • detects sources in every visit, links them across visits, and fits straight-line motion;
  • calibrates the position errors on the still stars of the same field;
  • keeps only motions that are at least 5σ significant, at least 0.3″ per year, and seen in at least three visits;
  • checks each motion against Gaia using the full direction and speed.

Each mover gets one of four labels:

  • known: a Gaia star moves the same way;
  • candidate: no Gaia star is on the track;
  • doubtful: saturated, or a Gaia star on the track moves differently;
  • unchecked: Gaia could not be reached.

It correctly recovers Barnard's Star (10.3″ per year) and Epsilon Indi B (4.4″ per year) as known. It flags WISE 0855, a cold brown dwarf that Gaia cannot see, as a candidate (7.5″ per year). The variable stars RW Aur and R Dra produce no false movers.

Benefits and intended impact

  • Anyone, from students to citizen scientists to astronomers, can explore SPHEREx data in seconds without installing software or knowing archive formats.
  • It makes discovery possible: SPHEREx maps the whole sky in infrared every six months, the light where cold nearby brown dwarfs are brightest. A moving source with no Gaia match is exactly what a new neighbour of the Sun would look like.
  • It stays current: new data releases are discovered automatically, "Check for new data" searches the archive again on request, and users can upload their own FITS images with sky coordinates (WCS) to explore other datasets the same way.

Tools and technologies

  • Science backend: Python, FastAPI, Astropy, NumPy, SciPy, reproject, and SEP for source extraction.
  • Data services: NASA/IPAC IRSA (image search), the SPHEREx archive on AWS S3, the ESA Gaia archive and VizieR (Gaia DR3, CatWISE2020), and CDS (Sesame name resolver, SIMBAD).
  • Frontend: React, TypeScript and Vite. Images are drawn with HTML canvas, alongside Aladin Lite.
  • Hosting: Cloudflare Workers (website and API), Cloudflare Containers (the Python science code) and R2 storage (cached results and saved image stacks).
  • Hardware: no special hardware; everything runs in the cloud and in any web browser.

Creativity

The tool combines a blink comparator, as used in classic brown-dwarf searches, with SPHEREx's unique spectroscopy: the same tool blinks through time and through wavelength. It turns "no Gaia match" into an automatic discovery signal, while an honest labelling system keeps artifacts from being presented as discoveries.

Factors we considered

  • Scientific honesty: one brightness scale across all frames, so changes are real; flagged and saturated data are marked rather than hidden; doubtful and unchecked results are labelled as such.
  • Speed: reading only the needed bytes is about 24 times faster than the archive's cutout service. Results are cached and survive updates, and the view on screen is processed first.
  • Ease of use: presets for the five challenge targets, clear legends, plain-language help, and a layout that works on phones.
  • Data that keeps arriving: new releases are picked up automatically.
  • Responsible operation: rate limits, private upload links deleted after 7 days, and credit to every data source.
